E6 — BJT Small-Signal I: Models, Fixed Bias and Bypassed Voltage-Divider CE (T6)

Why this matters in the exam: The mid-semester practice test stopped at DC bias. Its Q6–Q8 (22 of 50 marks) were BJT load lines and Q-points. Small-signal analysis is the next step on the same circuits, so expect it on the final. The Week 5 slides spend most of their length on it, WS6 Q1–Q11 are all small-signal, and Practical 3 was a bypassed voltage-divider CE amplifier. Every small-signal question begins with the DC Q-point ( gives ), so the 22 marks of DC skill carry straight into this topic. This pack covers the models and the two simplest CE circuits. Unbypassed , the emitter follower, CB, collector feedback and / loading are in E7.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Why we split DC and AC (superposition)

Every voltage and current is a DC part plus a signal part. The slides write this as and .

  • The DC part sets the Q-point. You find it from the DC circuit: capacitors open, signal source off.
  • The AC part is the signal. You find it from the small-signal circuit: capacitors shorted, DC sources grounded, BJT replaced by a linear model.

The BJT is not linear (), so superposition does not strictly apply. It works because the signal is small. Expanding the exponential gives

That first-order step is valid only for . The slides say “usually valid only for less than approximately 10 mV”. Within that range the BJT acts as a linear device. Its “gain constant” is the slope of the – curve at the Q-point. So the AC parameters depend on the DC current. That is why the DC analysis always comes first.

1.3 The models (they are the same circuit)

Hybrid-π (Sedra). Base to emitter: a resistor , with voltage across it. Collector to emitter: a current source pointing from collector to emitter, in parallel with . The slides show two forms of it: the VCCS form () and the CCCS form ().

model (Boylestad, CE). Base to emitter: a resistor . Collector to emitter: a current source in parallel with .

Why they are equivalent. Put in the hybrid-π model. Then , so

The input resistance and the controlled source are identical, so it is the same circuit with different labels. Pick whichever fits the question’s notation. Use Boylestad (, ) for “find , , ” questions, and Sedra (, ) when is given.

T model. Between base and emitter there is , and the controlled source (or ) runs from collector to base. It is handy when there is a resistor in the emitter, as in WS6 Q4 and pack E7.

h-parameters (Week 5, “Hybrid Equivalent Model”). The two-port equations are and . For CE these are . The slides drop (“normally a relatively small quantity”) to give the approximate hybrid model. Comparing it with the model gives:

1.4 The AC equivalent (slide 23, Week 5)

  1. Set all DC sources to zero (replace them with shorts). So becomes ground.
  2. Replace all capacitors (coupling , and bypass ) with shorts.
  3. Remove any element that a new short bypasses. A bypassed disappears.
  4. Redraw neatly, then replace the BJT with its model.

Consequence: (top at ) now runs from collector to ground. and now both run from base to ground, so they are in parallel: .

A rising raises , which raises and the drop , so falls. The minus sign in is that 180° shift. In WS6 Q3 it shows up directly: mV gives V.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Skipping the DC analysis. needs . Without a Q-point you have no , and every later mark is lost. Write the DC section even if it seems obvious.
  • Leaving in the AC circuit when bypasses it. Bypassed means AC-shorted. is in the DC analysis but not in or . (Unbypassed is E7, where .)
  • Taking to in the AC circuit. In AC, is ground, so goes collector-to-ground and goes base-to-ground, in parallel with .
  • Writing alone. The bias resistors are in parallel with the base: or . With a divider, often dominates. In Prac 3, was 8.2 kΩ against = 6.4 kΩ.
  • Dropping the minus sign or the phase statement. “” plus “180° phase shift” is the full answer. Some markers give a mark for the phase.
  • Ignoring when it is given. If the question gives , or , use it, or justify dropping it with . WS6 Q6’s S () gives kΩ, only 7× , which changes by 12 %.
  • Mixing = 25 and 26 mV, or and , within one answer. Pick one, state it, and stay with it. Round to no fewer than 4 significant figures before dividing.
  • Approximate VDB without the test. Check first. In WS6 Q6 it fails (396 kΩ < 560 kΩ). The approximate method gives Ω instead of 18.9 Ω, and the gain comes out about 10 % high.

WS6 Q5 (course question). The transistor amplifier shown in the figure 10 [the figure below; the sheet labels it Figure 5] is biased with a current source mA and has and V. Assuming that mA/V, and , answer the following questions:

Solution

1. The small-signal circuit. DC sources off and capacitors shorted:

  • in series with 2 kΩ drives the base; the 10 kΩ runs from base to ground.
  • Hybrid-π: from base to emitter; and from collector to emitter.
  • Z is grounded through its capacitor, so the emitter is at AC ground (the 1 mA source is open).
  • At the collector: the 8 kΩ (its top is AC ground) and the 8 kΩ load on Y, both to ground.

2. Gain. The output is the voltage across , with flowing into the collector from that network: is the voltage across , which forms a divider with the 2 kΩ source resistance: Numbers: = 2.016 kΩ, so the divider is 0.502. = 3.848 kΩ. An inverting amplifier.
